questions.q: What did “logos” mean to the Stoics?
a: The rational life force that gives order and purpose to everything
A method of logical argument used in Roman courts
The emperor’s written law that citizens had to obey
A state of calm achieved by avoiding all public duties
questions.why: Lesson 1 says logos is the essence of life and the master plan behind everything that happens.

questions.q: Why does Marcus Aurelius consider complaining pointless?
a: Everything is as it should be, and life is too short to waste
Complaining only works when speaking to someone in authority
Other people enjoy listening to complaints and feel closer
It relieves frustration faster than taking action does
questions.why: Lesson 2 argues that if everything is right as it is, complaining wastes limited time and spreads unhappiness.

questions.q: What did Marcus believe about harm that comes from an external source?
a: It is beyond your control and cannot truly harm you unless you allow it
It always leaves lasting damage that philosophy cannot address
It should be met with anger so others know your boundaries
It proves that the gods have abandoned the person involved
questions.why: Lesson 3 says external harm is outside your control; suffering begins only when you blame yourself or complain.

questions.q: How did Marcus Aurelius handle the deaths of his children and wife?
a: He trusted that they happened for a reason and stayed calm
He withdrew from his duties as emperor for years
He rejected Stoic philosophy and sought pleasure instead
He blamed his advisors for failing to protect them
questions.why: Lesson 3 says he accepted these losses as part of logos’s plan and remained calm in the worst times.

questions.q: What was the original purpose of the writings collected in Meditations?
a: They were private journals not intended for publication
They were official decrees addressed to the Roman Senate
They were lectures prepared for students of philosophy
They were letters written to a friend in Greece
questions.why: The overview says Marcus probably never meant these twelve books to be published; they were printed later.
